In this study, a high-resolution pollen record from the southwestern Iberian margin, combined with climate modeling, reveals a three-phase climate evolution linked to boreal summer insolation amplitude.
In the early phase ( ~ 1200–930 ka), strong insolation minima shifted westerlies north, boosting ice accumulation, while maxima promoted melting, limiting ice growth.
The middle phase ( ~ 930–790 ka) followed regoliths loss and featured weaker insolation extremes, leading to the southward migration of the westerlies, mega-droughts and greater ice buildup.

Multiple hypotheses have been proposed to explain this shift, including ice-sheet dynamics, such as ice-albedo feedbacks 3 , north-westerly driven precipitation at the ice margins 4 and the combined effect of CO 2 and insolation 5 , 6 .

A recent study observes a weak variation in both total and mean seasonal insolation around 800 ka due to a simultaneous weakening of the variation of precession and obliquity, and proposes this change in the astronomical forcing as a potential candidate to explain the MPT 9 .
This hypothesis and the associated mechanisms, in particular, changes in precipitation at the ice margins, remain however to be confirmed by proxy reconstructions and model simulations.

Here, we aim to reconstruct the evolution of precipitation in the mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere across the MPT, and test the role of insolation amplitude changes in driving the climate reorganization.

The Morlet wavelet is widely used in geophysical, climatological, and ecological applications 82 , 93 – 96 , as it provides an optimal balance between time and frequency localization 93 , 95 , 97 , 98 .

Furthermore, the Morlet wavelet has a simple and well-defined scale–frequency relationship ( f ~ 1/ s , where f is frequency and s is scale), which facilitates comparison with Fourier-based spectra and makes the identification of dominant periodicities more intuitive.
In discrete time, this integral is approximated through a convolution (via FFT) with appropriate zero-padding to mitigate edge effects (padding to next power-of-two length).

Bias correction and normalization The standard formulation of wavelet power is known to exhibit a bias toward smaller scales, as noted in several previous studies, and this bias is inherent to most existing implementations 82 , 93 , 101 , 102 .
To mitigate this limitation, we applied the bias-corrected normalization proposed of Liu et al., 103 which rescales the wavelet power to produce an unbiased representation of variance across scales.
This correction is implemented in the biwavelet R package 73 available freely from CRAN, which builds upon the MATLAB routines developed by Grinsted et al.

73 also refines the normalization of wavelet power relative to background spectra for both univariate and bivariate (cross-wavelet and coherence) analyses, thereby ensuring consistency and comparability between localized and global spectral measures.

Statistical significance and null models To assess whether observed spectral features (i.e., time-scale points) are statistically significant (i.e., exceed what would be expected under a null hypothesis of background variability), Torrence & Compo 82 derived the theoretical wavelet spectrum for red-noise processes, modeled as a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) process.
Under this null hypothesis/model, the expected wavelet power P null (s) and the associated confidence levels can be obtained from the chi-squared distribution with the appropriate degrees of freedom.
